findings.title: Client sends a new request to the project email address
findings.expected: The mail is received, classified, becomes a work item under the right engagement, and someone owns it.
findings.actual: Mailboxes and routing rules are configuration records in 3 files; 0 of those read them at runtime. Nothing receives mail.
findings.stops: at the first arrow — there is no inbound channel
findings.impact: The intake the product is named for cannot start. Every record is typed by hand.

findings.title: Client replies on an existing issue
findings.expected: The reply is recorded against the issue, the issue stops looking stale, and the trail shows who said what and when.
findings.actual: Note recorded, authored by "Validator", and the issue's last activity moved to 2026-08-15.
findings.stops: before the reply arrives on its own — the note is typed by a consultant, not received
findings.impact: The record is right once someone transcribes it. Nothing guarantees they do.

findings.title: Client sends an ambiguous request
findings.expected: The system marks it as needing clarification, asks the client, and does not start an SLA clock on work nobody has defined.
findings.actual: The status exists and the row reports health "Blocked" — blocked statuses are excluded from at-risk, so the issue stops being counted as slipping. The due date does not move: 2026-08-10 before, 2026-08-10 after. Waiting on a client consumes the same clock as working on it, and nothing asks the client anything.
findings.stops: at the clock — waiting on a client still consumes the SLA
findings.impact: Issues breach on client time. The report calls it our failure.

findings.title: Client sends an attachment
findings.expected: The file is stored, attached to the issue, and can be produced later as evidence.
findings.actual: The evidence record is created with kind, size and mime type (url: none). No bytes are stored — there is no upload path anywhere in the source.
findings.stops: at the file itself — the record describes an artefact the system does not hold
findings.impact: Evidence cannot be produced at a governance meeting. The list of it can.

findings.title: The same defect is reported twice
findings.expected: The duplicate is detected, linked to the original, and does not become a second stream of work.
findings.actual: The link and the Superseded status both work, closing sets actualEnd to 2026-08-15, and the transition graph makes the duplicate call an explained one — Superseded needs a reason, which is now on the trail. Detection is still manual: the duplicate-detection agent is a registry record with no runtime.
findings.stops: at detection — a person must notice
findings.impact: Duplicates are found late, after two people have worked the same fault.

findings.title: An issue needs another consultant to help
findings.expected: A contributor can be added without taking ownership, and the trail shows both.
findings.actual: The mechanism works: an unbounded responsibility holds 2 people, the owner is still Priya, and the change is audited. But the shipped operating model has 3 responsibilities — Owner, Accountable Party, Raised By — and 0 of them accept more than one name. Contributor is a type the firm must invent.
findings.stops: at the shipped model — helping is possible, but not offered
findings.impact: Out of the box, the only way to involve a second person is to hand over ownership.

findings.title: Work is assigned to someone who is not available
findings.expected: The system refuses, or warns, because that person is on leave or already committed.
findings.actual: Accepted without comment. The owner is now "Someone Who Does Not Exist" — a name that is not in the people directory, let alone free. Owner is a free-text column, not a reference.
findings.stops: at the first check — there is none
findings.impact: Work can be assigned to a leaver, a typo, or someone with no capacity, and nothing notices.

findings.title: A consultant is already overallocated
findings.expected: Assigning more work surfaces the conflict before it is committed.
findings.actual: No allocation, capacity or availability record exists (a type exists). Capacity in the estimator is three numbers typed on one issue.
findings.stops: at the entity — there is nothing to be over
findings.impact: The plan cannot be checked against the people who have to deliver it.

findings.title: New work arrives and there is not enough capacity for it
findings.expected: The delivery plan is shown to be impossible before it is agreed.
findings.actual: Requires L. The estimator can say an issue needs 40 hours; nothing knows whether 40 hours exist.
findings.stops: at the same missing entity
findings.impact: Commitments are made against capacity nobody has counted.

findings.title: An issue approaches its SLA target
findings.expected: It is flagged at risk before it breaches, and the person who can act is told.
findings.actual: Health computes as "At Risk" from dates and progress, and the grid shows it. Nobody is told, and the reason is now sharper than "no notifications exist": notifications and rules both exist, and every rule reacts to something that *changed*. Becoming at risk is not a change — it is the passage of time against a date that has not moved — so there is no event for a rule to subscribe to.
findings.stops: at the clock — automation is event-driven, and going at-risk is something that happens by time passing rather than by anybody doing anything
findings.impact: At-risk work is still found by opening the app. A scheduled pass is the missing piece, not a channel.

findings.title: An issue breaches its SLA
findings.expected: It is overdue, it is escalated to the accountable party, and it appears on the report.
findings.actual: Health is "Overdue" and the daily IMS lists it under "Overdue". Escalation could now be expressed as a rule — telling a role is one action away — but nothing fires it, because a breach is a date passing rather than a change anybody made.
findings.stops: at the same clock as H — the machinery to route a breach exists, and nothing wakes up to notice one
findings.impact: A breach reaches a report, not a person with authority to fix it.

findings.title: A project milestone becomes at risk
findings.expected: The milestone shows the risk, and it rolls up to the project so a governance meeting sees it.
findings.actual: A late issue rolls up: its process area now reports 2026-08-01 → 2026-08-09 with 17% complete. Milestones exist as a row kind, but no milestone record ties to a SOW or a payment.
findings.stops: at the milestone as a commercial object
findings.impact: Delivery risk is visible; contractual consequence is not.

findings.title: A consultant records time against an issue
findings.expected: The hours land on the work item, move it off stale, and become the actual half of the estimate.
findings.actual: 5.5h recorded across 2 activities — 3.5h billable, 2h not — and the issue is no longer stale (last activity 2026-08-15). Refused: a future day ("Time cannot be recorded for a day that has not happened."), an 18-hour entry, and 1.37 hours. Removing an entry withdraws it rather than destroying it.
findings.stops: at money — hours are recorded, and a rate to multiply them by does not exist anywhere
findings.impact: Actual effort, variance and utilisation now have a source. Cost and margin still do not.

findings.title: Somebody logs hours in a colleague's name
findings.expected: It is refused unless they hold the grant for it, because hours are that person's account of their own day.
findings.actual: A consultant logging their own hours is fine; logging Sam's is refused — "Record others' time is not something Functional Consultant can do here. Time is recorded by the person who did the work." A project manager holds the grant and may, and the entry keeps Sam's name while the trail records who typed it.
findings.impact: Hours cannot be attributed to somebody who did not agree they worked them, except by a role the firm chose to trust with it.

findings.title: Actual effort overruns the estimate
findings.expected: The variance is visible on the issue, and it is honest about what it is measured against.
findings.actual: 12h spent against 8h agreed — +4h, 50%. An unestimated issue reports its variance as unknown rather than as an overrun against zero, and an overrun against a draft is labelled as such: a number nobody agreed is not a commitment anybody broke.
findings.stops: before it reaches the project — the variance is per issue, and nothing rolls it up to a milestone, a SOW or a margin
findings.impact: A consultant can see the overrun on the record. A partner still cannot see it on the engagement.

findings.title: A client asks for something outside the SOW
findings.expected: The system can tell that it is outside — and if it cannot judge that, it can at least show what the request costs against what was agreed.
findings.actual: 18h of 40h used (45%), and the current plan needs 54h — 14h more than was agreed. The overrun is arithmetic rather than opinion: agreed effort is on the SOW, planned comes from the estimates, spent comes from the recorded hours. A project attributed to nothing is counted as such (1 here), and a draft SOW refuses work: "SOW-2026-015 is draft. Work cannot be delivered under it yet."
findings.stops: at the judgement — nothing reads the scope statement and decides whether a particular request is inside it
findings.impact: Scope leakage is now measurable where it shows up as effort. Whether a request is in scope remains a commercial call, and the product makes its consequence visible rather than pretending to make the call.

findings.title: A change request is raised
findings.expected: It is captured as a CR, valued, and linked to the work it changes.
findings.actual: A CR can be raised as a work item of type "Change Request" — the type is configuration and had to be added first, linked to the issue that prompted it, and it cannot start until somebody with the authority approves it (scenario P). What it still carries is no value of its own: approving it does not move the agreed effort or value on the statement of work, so a firm sees the overrun rather than the amendment.
findings.stops: at valuation — approval is built, and an approved change still does not amend the SOW it changes
findings.impact: A CR is a note about money, not a control over it.

findings.title: A change request is approved
findings.expected: The approval is given by somebody with the authority for it, and the work cannot start without it.
findings.actual: Unapproved, the CR cannot start: "Change request approval is needed before this can move to “In Progress”." The consultant who asked cannot answer — "Decide an approval is not something Functional Consultant can do here." — and neither can an analyst, because the rule names the sponsor: "Decide an approval is not something Support Analyst can do here." Once the sponsor approves, the work starts. A rejection blocks the same move and stays on the record: "Change request approval: this was rejected by Dana. Not within this phase — raise it for the next release."
findings.stops: at the commercial consequence — approving a change does not move a SOW value, because there is no SOW
findings.impact: A change can no longer be delivered without somebody with authority agreeing to it. What it is worth is still not recorded anywhere.

findings.title: A firm writes an approval rule that nobody can satisfy
findings.expected: The rule is refused, rather than becoming a wall the work never gets past.
findings.actual: A rule with no decider is refused — "“Impossible” names no role that can decide it, so nothing it gates could ever proceed." — and so is one that asks nothing: "“Unasked” asks no question. Somebody has to be told what they are approving." Both would produce work that reaches a status never, and whoever wrote the rule would hear about it weeks later from somebody who could not proceed.
findings.impact: A control that cannot be satisfied is a wall, and the configuration screen refuses to build one.

findings.title: An issue is closed with no evidence attached
findings.expected: Closure is refused, because the resolution could not be produced later.
findings.actual: Refused without evidence: "“Closed - confirmed” needs at least one piece of evidence on the record — that is what makes the closure producible later." Accepted once a sign-off document is attached. Closing as "no defect" needs no evidence but does need a reason, because it makes a claim about the work rather than about the client.
findings.impact: A confirmed closure now has something behind it that can be shown to a client who disputes it.

findings.title: Work is closed as “no defect” with no explanation
findings.expected: The change is refused until somebody says why, and the why survives on the trail.
findings.actual: Refused without a reason: "“Closed - no defect” needs a reason. This is the outcome people ask about months later." With one, the change lands and the trail carries it — "Behaviour is as designed; raised against an out-of-date specification.". The reason is stamped only on the status entry, so a closure rationale is never attributed to an unrelated field in the same save.
findings.impact: The two closures a client queries later now come with the firm’s own explanation attached.

findings.title: An issue is resolved
findings.expected: The resolution is recorded, the client is told, and verification is requested.
findings.actual: The status moves, the next action is recorded and 2 audit entries were written with before, after and actor. No message is sent to the client.
findings.stops: at telling the client
findings.impact: Verification waits on somebody remembering to ask for it.

findings.title: An issue is verified and closed
findings.expected: Closure is recorded with a date, and it cannot be reopened without a trace.
findings.actual: Reached along the route the graph requires — In Progress, Awaiting client confirmation, evidence attached, then closed. Closing derived actualEnd = 2026-08-15; reopening cleared it, and both derived writes are in the trail (2 entries). The derivation guards on the status having changed, so an unrelated edit cannot overwrite a closure date.
findings.impact: Closure and reopening are both honest about the date.

findings.title: An issue jumps straight from Open to Closed, skipping every intermediate state
findings.expected: The transition is refused, and the refusal says where the work can actually go from here.
findings.actual: Refused: "“Open” cannot move straight to “Closed - confirmed”. From here the work can go to: In Progress, Needs clarification, Closed - no defect, Superseded." The same move succeeds along the route the graph allows — In Progress, Awaiting client confirmation, then Closed - confirmed with evidence attached. A patch carrying a refused status is rejected whole, so the other fields in it are not quietly saved.
findings.impact: Closure now requires the steps that make it defensible, and the graph is configuration a firm can change.

findings.title: A firm turns transition enforcement off
findings.expected: Every move is allowed again, and the change is recorded as the decision it is.
findings.actual: With enforcement off the direct close is accepted again, and the switch is audited with before and after. A table that would trap work is refused rather than saved: "Work in “In Progress” could never be closed — no route from it reaches a closing status."
findings.impact: The control is the firm’s to relax, and relaxing it is a recorded decision rather than a silent default.

findings.title: A consultant, an analyst and a client user each try the same nine operations
findings.expected: Each is allowed what their role grants and refused the rest, with a refusal that explains itself.
findings.actual: Consultant may raise, edit, close, reopen, schedule and estimate but not archive or configure. Analyst may raise, edit and note but not close, reopen, schedule or estimate — reopening counts as a closure decision, because it moves a record back out of the done set. Client user may raise and note only. The refusal names the role rather than just saying no: "Close work is not something Client User can do here."
findings.impact: The rules a firm states about who may do what are now applied, and applied at the reducer rather than in the screens.

findings.title: Somebody claims to be a colleague
findings.expected: The claim is verified against an identity provider before anything is allowed.
findings.actual: No authentication exists: no session, no token verification, no provider. Every request resolves to one operator read from an environment variable, so authorisation is enforced against a claimed identity rather than a proven one. The permission model stops a mistake, not an attacker — the code says so where it is defined.
findings.stops: at proving who somebody is
findings.impact: Grants are only as good as the claim behind them. Until a login exists, the fallback role is effectively everyone.

findings.title: Somebody edits another person's note
findings.expected: The edit is refused, because a note is that person's account — unless they hold the supervisor grant.
findings.actual: Refused for a different author: "Written by Validator. A note is that person's account of what they saw, so it is theirs to correct." With the supervisor grant it lands, and the note still says it was written by Validator while recording Someone Else as the editor. The rule had existed in the panel since notes shipped and was never checked in the reducer — so it held for people using the button and for nothing else that could dispatch.
findings.impact: Somebody else's account of what they saw can no longer be rewritten under their name — provided they hold a role of their own. An actor with none still falls back to Administrator, which is ST2b.

findings.title: Two people edit the same issue at once
findings.expected: The second write is detected as conflicting rather than silently overwriting the first.
findings.actual: Both writes apply. Replaying the first against the second's state succeeds silently — owner ends as "Priya". There is no version, no row hash and no If-Match: the reducer rejects impossible states, not stale ones. Result: last writer wins, and only the audit trail shows the loss.
findings.stops: at concurrency control
findings.impact: Two consultants working the same issue overwrite each other. The trail records it; neither is told.

findings.title: A record is archived and later restored
findings.expected: Nothing is orphaned, and anything moved out during the archive comes back.
findings.actual: Restoring a child under an archived parent is refused ("“Inventory” is archived, so this would be restored somewhere nothing can see it. Restore that first."), and restoring the parent brings all 3 records back. Deletion is soft throughout; nothing is destroyed.
findings.impact: The data lifecycle is reversible and cannot produce an unreachable record.

findings.title: The firm shortens its High-severity SLA from 5 days to 2
findings.expected: The next issue raised gets a 2-day target, and everything downstream follows.
findings.actual: Default High = 5d proposed 2026-08-10; after the change the same issue proposes 2026-08-05. The policy is read from the model at every derivation, not captured at startup, and the change is audited with before and after.
findings.impact: Configuration reaches runtime for the SLA. Dates already committed are deliberately left alone, and the screen says so.

findings.title: The firm adds a work type and retires another
findings.expected: New records can use the new type, and records already filed under the retired one stay readable.
findings.actual: A new type is usable immediately (true), and retiring one in use is refused: "3 records are classified as "Defect". Reclassify them first.".
findings.impact: The discriminator behaves as configuration, which is what keeps one work-item table honest.

findings.title: A project is created from a template
findings.expected: Work items, workflow, SLA, notifications, agents and checklists all arrive with it.
findings.actual: Adopting "Axiocloud standard delivery" at a scope works and carries 6 agents, 2 workflows, an approval default. It creates no work items, applies no SLA of its own and configures no notifications — a template is a set of defaults, not a project setup.
findings.stops: at everything the template does not carry
findings.impact: Mobilising a project is still manual; only the operating-model defaults are inherited.

findings.title: The daily IMS report is checked against the records it counts
findings.expected: Every figure on the report can be reproduced from the underlying rows.
findings.actual: Report says open=2 and overdue=1; recounting the rows gives 2 and 1. Section "Overdue" lists 1. The report derives from the same rows the grid shows, counts rather than estimates, and prints its own section cap rather than truncating silently.
findings.impact: The one report that exists reconciles to its source.

findings.title: Weekly client and monthly governance reporting
findings.expected: A client-safe weekly pack and a monthly governance pack can be produced.
findings.actual: Only the daily IMS is built (1 report module(s) in source). The weekly pack needs a client-visible boundary that does not exist — no field marks a record or a note as client-safe.
findings.stops: at the visibility boundary
findings.impact: Anything sent to a client is assembled by hand, and internal notes are one copy-paste from the client.

findings.title: Every meaningful change answers who, what, when, before, after and why
findings.expected: The trail is complete enough to defend a decision months later.
findings.actual: 2 entries, all carrying actor, time, field, before and after; 1 carry a reason. Attribution is a parameter of the reducer, so no action can forge it — proven separately by audit:attribution. Why is captured where the product asks for it (date changes, estimate revisions) and absent elsewhere.
findings.stops: at "why" for ordinary field edits
findings.impact: The trail is strong on what changed, thinner on the reasoning behind routine edits.

findings.title: The assistant proposes a change with low confidence
findings.expected: It recommends rather than acts, and a person decides.
findings.actual: One live agent exists behind a chat route, and its proposals are rendered as cards a person accepts or rejects (11 files participate). Confidence thresholds and autonomy levels are registry fields with no runtime that reads them. Driving it needs a model key this script does not have.
findings.stops: at the autonomy fields — declared, unread
findings.impact: 37 of 38 agents are records. The one that runs is gated correctly, but the gate is code, not the configured policy.

findings.title: The database is unreachable while someone is working
findings.expected: The user keeps working, nothing is lost, and the queue recovers when it comes back.
findings.actual: The queue retries with backoff four times, then halts and tells the user — and never resumes: nothing ever clears the halt for the life of the session. Editing continues into the local mirror, so work is visible but unsaved. Separately, the unload flush sends the first 50 queued actions and then clears the whole queue, dropping the remainder.
findings.stops: at recovery
findings.impact: A ten-second outage silently ends persistence for the rest of the session.

findings.title: A malformed or hostile write reaches the API
findings.expected: It is rejected before it touches stored state.
findings.actual: The endpoint validates the batch shape and the action kind against an allowlist, resolves tenant and actor server-side, and refuses anything else. It does not validate the payload: an action's fields are spread into the record, and TypeScript is erased at runtime. The reducer catches impossible values it knows about; it does not police unknown keys.
findings.stops: at field-level validation
findings.impact: Today the endpoint is unauthenticated anyway, so this is latent. It becomes the sharp edge the moment identity lands.

findings.title: The persistence layer is exercised at all
findings.expected: Writes reach Postgres and reload correctly.
findings.actual: DATABASE_URL is not set, and there is no .env.example. The repository, mappers, write path and baseline migration exist across 1 module(s) and typecheck, but no test in this repository has ever run them against a database. Every proof here is reducer-level.
findings.stops: at the database — it has never been connected in this environment
findings.impact: The most reversible-looking layer is the least verified. A mapper mistake would surface as data loss on first deployment.

findings.title: A consultant submits a timesheet
findings.expected: The week is presented for approval, and approval freezes exactly what was approved.
findings.actual: Entries exist and are the record, and approvals exist and gate transitions — but nothing gathers entries into a period to be approved (no such type in source). The two halves are built; the join is not. The entry-as-record decision is what makes that join non-trivial: an approval will have to name the entries it covered, or an edit afterwards silently changes an approved total.
findings.stops: at the period — approval itself now exists and gates transitions; nothing gathers a week of entries to put in front of it
findings.impact: Time is recorded and cannot yet be signed off, so it cannot be billed.

findings.title: A submitted timesheet is rejected
findings.expected: The rejection returns specific entries, says why, and the corrected resubmission is traceable.
findings.actual: Requires U. The nearest existing mechanism is the estimate revision log, which refuses to let an agreed number move without a reason — the same shape this needs, applied to a different record.
findings.stops: at the same missing approval
findings.impact: No correction loop exists for the record that drives revenue.

findings.title: A notification fails to deliver
findings.expected: The failure is visible and recorded — a silent non-delivery is the dangerous case.
findings.actual: The message is recorded with an outcome rather than attempted and lost: delivery is "pending" because "No email transport is configured, so this was recorded and not sent." The count of undelivered messages is shown in the inbox and on the automation screen to everybody, rather than hidden behind a setting — a firm that configured email escalation and has never sent one should not discover it from a client asking why nobody called.
findings.stops: at the transport — in-app is delivered because the inbox is the delivery; email and Teams have nowhere to go
findings.impact: Non-delivery is visible and counted. It is still non-delivery: nothing leaves the building.

findings.title: The assistant recommends something wrong
findings.expected: A person rejects it, the rejection is recorded, and the original recommendation is preserved.
findings.actual: Proposals are rendered as cards a person accepts or rejects (3 chat module(s) implement it), and an accepted proposal goes through the same reducer as a human edit, so it is audited identically. A rejection changes nothing and is recorded nowhere — no rejection log exists in source — so the system cannot learn which recommendations were wrong.
findings.stops: at the rejection — it disappears
findings.impact: Agent quality cannot be measured, because only the accepted half of its output is kept.

findings.title: An automation fails part-way through
findings.expected: The run stops safely, what did happen is visible, and the failure is recorded rather than swallowed.
findings.actual: The working step ran and the impossible one did not: 1 notification raised, 1 step refused ("That approval rule no longer exists."), and the original change stands. A rule addressed to a role nobody holds reports it — "Reached nobody — "role:ROLE_CLIENT_SPONSOR" resolves to no one in the directory." — rather than looking like it worked. Rules act by dispatching ordinary actions, so a rule cannot do anything a person could not, and everything it does is in the trail with the rule that caused it.
findings.stops: at the schedule — every rule reacts to something that happened, so "every morning, escalate what is about to breach" cannot be expressed
findings.impact: Event-driven automation works and fails safely. Time-driven automation needs a clock and a process to run it, and this application has neither.

findings.title: An integration fails
findings.expected: The failure is contained, retried where safe, surfaced, and never leaves records half-written.
findings.actual: No outbound integration exists. The only network call the product makes is to the model behind the chat route; no DevOps, SharePoint or Teams client appears in source.
findings.stops: at the integration
findings.impact: Nothing to fail yet — but the write path has no idempotency key, so retries will need one before the first integration lands. See FL4.

findings.title: The same write is delivered twice
findings.expected: The second delivery is recognised and ignored, rather than creating a second record.
findings.actual: Replaying an identical action produces 2 records, because ids are minted server-side from the workspace counter and nothing identifies a request — there is no idempotency key. The unload flush makes this reachable rather than theoretical: a beacon fires on visibilitychange and can re-send a batch that is already in flight.
findings.stops: at request identity
findings.impact: Hiding a tab mid-save can duplicate notes, evidence and dependencies. The user sees two of something they did once.

findings.title: An issue changes owner, and eight dependent areas should follow
findings.expected: Work, capacity, notifications, activity history, audit, reporting and AI context all reflect the new owner.
findings.actual: 4 of 8 dependent areas follow the change — the work item, the audit trail, activity history, the daily report. The other four are absent rather than stale: resource workload, capacity, notifications, AI context. Nothing derived is stored, so within the areas that exist there is no drift to find: the report recomputes from the same rows the grid does.
findings.stops: at the four areas that have no entity behind them
findings.impact: Propagation is correct as far as it goes. It goes half as far as the operating model describes.
